name: Boron + zinc + D3 test-boost stack

card.summary: Boron, zinc and D3 together as a testosterone stack: each has a plausible hormone link, but the combo has no trial behind it.
card.note: Zinc beyond sufficiency does not raise testosterone, per Wikipedia.

quick.overview:
A popular supplement stack of boron, zinc and vitamin D3 taken to raise testosterone.

Deficiency of zinc or vitamin D is linked to lower levels; evidence for the stack in people without deficiency was not found.
quick.mechanism: Zinc supports testosterone synthesis, vitamin D intake correlates with higher levels, and boron is proposed to influence steroid metabolism.
quick.risks: Borates have low mammalian toxicity per Wikipedia, but excess intake of any ingredient is not covered in the sources reviewed.

lead: The boron, zinc and vitamin D3 stack is a combination of over-the-counter supplements taken together in the belief that they support testosterone. Users pursue it for the look that goes with higher testosterone: easier muscle gain, leaner body composition and the fuller-looking physique associated with it. The three ingredients are cheap, widely sold and have each been studied for a connection to male hormone physiology.

Zinc is required to produce testosterone, and zinc deficiency can lower circulating testosterone and delay puberty [1]. Boron is an ultratrace element; a 2008 review in the Journal of Dietary Supplements listed hormone regulation and bodybuilding (increasing testosterone) among nine indications for which it is popularly used, while noting a lack of systematic study in humans [2]. A 2015 review argues boron affects how the body uses estrogen, testosterone and vitamin D [3]. Vitamin D intake has been associated with testosterone levels in the literature summarized by Wikipedia [4].

On looksmax.org, boron in particular is discussed as a supplement for testosterone and for 'heightmaxxing', with posts quoting a small study in eight healthy men that reported higher free testosterone and lower estradiol after a week of boron [5]. No published trial has tested the three-ingredient stack as a combination.

chain: Supplement a mineral and vitamin tied to testosterone production
Support testosterone, particularly where intake is low
angle.text: People take the stack hoping for higher testosterone and the muscle, leanness and recovery that go with it. Each ingredient has a documented link to hormone physiology, and zinc deficiency is known to lower testosterone [1].

paras: Zinc is required to produce testosterone. Deficiency can reduce circulating testosterone and cause hypogonadism and delayed puberty, and a 1963 case report described a young man with infantile genitalia and stunted growth whose symptoms reversed with zinc [1].
Wikipedia's testosterone article reports that vitamin D intakes in the range of roughly 400 to 1,000 IU per day were associated with higher testosterone, as intake-level correlations [4].

Boron is only needed in traces by plants and borates have low toxicity in mammals [6]. The 2008 review says humans ingest it through food and that systematic study of its safety and effectiveness in humans was lacking [2]. A 2015 review lists reported roles in bone, wound healing, magnesium absorption and inflammatory markers as well as the body's use of sex hormones [3]. A review of boric acid, borax and other boron compounds notes that high exposure can cause toxic effects and that fatalities have occurred after large oral or skin exposure to boric acid [7].

A looksmax.org introductory thread presents boron as a supplement for height and testosterone and quotes a study in eight healthy males reporting a rise in free testosterone from about 11.8 to 15.2 pg/mL and a fall in estradiol after one week [5]. Another thread asks whether boron raises DHT and hair loss; one user says he felt strong effects on libido and lifting, and others ask whether his hair loss worsened [8]. Boron also appears in forum lists alongside prescription testosterone regimens [9].

No studies found of the three-ingredient combination. Research exists on single nutrients: the 2008 boron review discusses boron for testosterone as one of nine popular uses [2], and the 2015 review summarizes reported effects of boron on sex hormones [3].

lore.intro: Boron, zinc and D3 are discussed on looksmax.org as inexpensive supplements to support testosterone, with boron also linked to height and hair loss questions [5][8].

claims.experts: No published study was found that tests boron against hair loss.
